title: Rapid economic and human-capital gains can coexist with fragile youth transition, high work pressure, loneliness, gender barriers, and declining trust
source_unit: OECD, Inclusive and Sustainable Well-being in Korea: 30 Years of OECD Membership and Future Policy Opportunities
geography: Republic of Korea, benchmarked against OECD countries and tracked from Korea’s 1996 OECD membership where data allow, with breakdowns by gender, age, and education

observations.period: 1996-2022; Korea’s three decades of OECD membership

denominator.unit: Korea’s national well-being trajectory benchmarked against OECD peers

life_expectancy.value: nearly 83 years in 2022, over 8 years higher than in 1996 and almost 2 years above the OECD average

road_safety.unit: percent reduction in road deaths since 1996

education.value: 25-34 year-olds have the highest secondary and tertiary completion rates in the OECD

material_progress.value: the household-income gap with the OECD average halved between 2004 and 2022, while child poverty fell from well above to among the lowest OECD rates

observations.method: OECD multidimensional well-being framework combining aggregate trends, peer benchmarking, population-group inequalities, and Korea-specific quality-of-life data.
observations.uncertainty: The report is descriptive and policy-oriented; trends across well-being dimensions do not establish that economic growth caused each improvement or that Korea’s trajectory transfers to other countries.
observations.subgroup: Korean households, children, young adults, older people, women and men, and groups differentiated by age and education.
observations.counterinterpretation: Aggregate progress is substantial and should not be obscured by current problems; the central analytical question is distribution, sustainability, and whether gains persist across generations.

observations.period: 2020-2022; transition from education to economic independence

denominator.unit: Korean young-adult transition context compared with OECD peers

parental_co_residence.unit: percent of 20-29 year-olds living with parents in Korea in 2020

oecd_comparison.unit: percent of 20-29 year-olds living with parents across the OECD in 2022

transition_pressure.value: young people face difficulty accessing secure, skill-matched work and wages that keep pace with high living costs

policy_bundle.value: youth support needs to integrate skills and employability with financial stability, housing, mental health, social connection, and civic participation

observations.method: Life-course and age-group analysis within the OECD well-being framework, connected to labor, housing, income, mental-health, and civic-participation policy evidence.
observations.uncertainty: Living with parents is not inherently a welfare deficit and may reflect cultural preferences, housing costs, family support, or life-stage timing; the report does not identify one causal driver.
observations.subgroup: Young Korean adults, students, job-seekers, young workers, parents, households facing housing and cost pressure, and people transitioning into independent adulthood.
observations.counterinterpretation: Intergenerational co-residence can provide material and care support; the policy concern is constrained choice when secure work, housing, and social participation are difficult to access.

observations.period: 2026; social capital, mental health, and life-course connection

denominator.unit: Korean population life-course and OECD comparison frame

government_trust.value: lower than the OECD average and declining in recent years

suicide_position.value: Korea has the highest suicide rate in the OECD, with rising child and adolescent suicide trends highlighted as a continuing concern

older_support.value: 61% of Korean men and 65% of Korean women aged 70 and over report having someone to count on in a time of need, compared with OECD averages of 89% and 87%

youth_connection.value: youth loneliness is rising alongside broader mental-health and transition pressures

observations.method: OECD analysis of social connections, mental health, institutional trust, and age-group outcomes using international and national indicators.
observations.uncertainty: The indicators are not a single measure of social capital or mental health, and the report does not establish a causal pathway from trust or loneliness to suicide or other outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Young people, older adults, Korean men and women, job-seekers, workers, and people with limited social support or access to mental-health care.
observations.counterinterpretation: Strong family and community relationships may be under-measured by standardized support questions; high recorded need can also reflect improved detection and help-seeking.

work_time.unit: hours more worked per year by Korean workers than the OECD average

gender_barrier.value: persistent gender wage, employment, leadership, unpaid-work, and gender-role gaps

gender_based_violence.unit: percent of Korean women aged 15 and over reporting intimate-partner violence in 2018, compared with an OECD average of 4%

natural_capital.value: per-capita greenhouse-gas emissions and carbon footprint are among the highest across OECD countries

policy_implication.value: well-being policy requires cross-sector coordination, equity, inclusion, and long-term prevention rather than sector reforms alone

observations.method: OECD structural analysis linking labor, unpaid care, gender, violence, environment, and policy-practice principles.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies coexisting pressures and policy opportunities; it does not estimate the causal effect of work hours, gender norms, or carbon intensity on each well-being outcome.
observations.subgroup: Korean women and men, caregivers, workers, young and older adults, survivors of gender-based violence, and future generations exposed to environmental costs.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rapid growth and long work hours may have supported past material gains, while gender and environmental reforms could improve well-being without reversing economic capability if designed with transition support.

related_sources.claim: Official 209-page OECD report PDF with aggregate, life-course, gender, social-capital, environmental, and policy chapters.
Official OECD DOI and publication citation.

boundary: This record adds a growth-to-lived-well-being and life-course-distribution route. It is not a causal evaluation of Korea’s growth model, a universal theory of Asian development, a respondent-level mental-health study, or proof that any recommended policy package will improve trust, connection, gender equality, or youth independence.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official OECD publication page and 209-page report PDF were reviewed for long-run human-capital and material gains, youth transition, trust, suicide and social-support patterns, work-time, gender barriers, violence, carbon intensity, and cross-sector policy principles.
